title: What is the difference between `repartition(n)` and `coalesce(n)` — repartition is a wide transformation (full shuffle, round-robin, can increase or decrease partitions, produces evenly-sized output) vs coalesce is a narrow transformation (no shuffle, stitches existing partitions, can only decrease, output is unevenly sized)?

s1_definition.profdef: Both `repartition(n)` and `coalesce(n)` change the number of partitions, but they work very differently. `repartition(n)` is a wide transformation that performs a full shuffle, redistributing all records across the network round-robin into exactly n evenly-sized partitions, and it can either increase or decrease the partition count. `coalesce(n)` is a narrow transformation that performs no shuffle, instead stitching existing partitions together on the same executors, which can only decrease the partition count and produces unevenly-sized output.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine transaction files split across clerks' desks at the National Bank of India. Repartition is dumping every file into the middle of the room and redealing them evenly into exactly the number of new piles you want — fair and balanced, but everyone has to carry their files across the room, which is slow. Coalesce is just asking a few clerks to slide their existing piles together into fewer stacks without anyone walking anywhere — fast and cheap, but the resulting stacks are whatever sizes the original piles happened to be, so they can be lopsided, and you can only ever end up with fewer stacks, never more.
s1_definition.oneliner: `repartition(n)` fully shuffles into n evenly-sized partitions and can increase or decrease, while `coalesce(n)` merges existing partitions with no shuffle, only decreases, and can be uneven.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Both `repartition(n)` and `coalesce(n)` change the number of partitions, but they work very differently. `repartition(n)` is a wide transformation that performs a full shuffle, redistributing all records across the network round-robin into exactly n evenly-sized partitions, and it can either increase or decrease the partition count. `coalesce(n)` is a narrow transformation that performs no shuffle, instead stitching existing partitions together on the same executors, which can only decrease the partition count and produces unevenly-sized output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine transaction files split across clerks' desks at the National Bank of India. Repartition is dumping every file into the middle of the room and redealing them evenly into exactly the number of new piles you want — fair and balanced, but everyone has to carry their files across the room, which is slow. Coalesce is just asking a few clerks to slide their existing piles together into fewer stacks without anyone walking anywhere — fast and cheap, but the resulting stacks are whatever sizes the original piles happened to be, so they can be lopsided, and you can only ever end up with fewer stacks, never more.

**One line to remember:** `repartition(n)` fully shuffles into n evenly-sized partitions and can increase or decrease, while `coalesce(n)` merges existing partitions with no shuffle, only decreases, and can be uneven.

sections.s2_technical:
Repartition is a wide transformation, which means it triggers a full shuffle. Every record is sent across the network and distributed round-robin into the requested number of partitions, so the output is evenly balanced regardless of how skewed the input was. Because it is a true shuffle, repartition can do anything: increase the partition count, decrease it, or keep it the same while rebalancing. The cost is the shuffle itself — network transfer, disk writes, and serialization — so repartition is expensive, but you get perfectly even partitions out of it, which is exactly what you want before a heavy parallel stage or to fix skew.

Coalesce is a narrow transformation when it is reducing partitions, which means no shuffle. Instead of redistributing records, it logically combines existing partitions by assigning several parent partitions to each resulting partition on the same executor, so data does not move across the network. This makes coalesce very cheap. The trade-offs follow directly from the no-shuffle design: coalesce can only decrease the partition count, because without a shuffle it cannot create new partitions or move records to balance them, and the output can be uneven, because it simply stitches together whatever partitions existed, so if those were different sizes the merged ones are too.

The classic use cases make the choice clear. You use coalesce to reduce partitions cheaply after a heavy filter, for example when a job filtered a large dataset down to a small slice spread across two hundred partitions and you want to write it out as a few files without paying for a shuffle. You use repartition when you need balanced partitions — before an expensive stage so every task has equal work, to increase parallelism by raising the partition count, or to deliberately rebalance skewed data. A common writing pattern is coalesce to one for a single output file when the data is small, but repartition when the data is large so the write is parallelized and balanced.

A senior nuance is that coalesce reducing to very few partitions can backfire, because it also reduces the parallelism of the stage that produces the data: if you coalesce to one before an expensive computation, that whole computation runs in a single task. In that case you either coalesce after the heavy work or use repartition to keep parallelism while controlling output. Another nuance is that coalesce with a larger number than the current partition count has no effect unless you pass the shuffle flag, which turns it into a repartition. In the bank, I used coalesce to tidy up the many tiny partitions left after filtering a daily slice before writing it, and repartition to rebalance before a heavy join or to raise parallelism on a large skewed dataset.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — After filtering, a dataset has many tiny partitions and must be written as a few files cheaply. This is exactly coalesce — reduce with no shuffle.

Problem 2 — Before a heavy join, partitions are unbalanced and tasks would be uneven. This is exactly repartition — full shuffle into even partitions.

Problem 3 — The team must understand that coalesce can be uneven and only decreases, while repartition is even and can increase. This is exactly the trade-off to demonstrate.

The mini-project models both in Java. A `Partitioner` exposes `repartition`, which redistributes all records round-robin into exactly n even partitions and reports a shuffle, and `coalesce`, which merges existing partitions with no shuffle, only decreasing, and reports the resulting uneven sizes. The demo starts from skewed partitions of Rajesh's and Priya's transactions and shows both operations and their costs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three skewed partitions — one with six of Rajesh's transactions and two with one transaction each, eight records total that are badly unbalanced.

Step 1: Repartition to two is called. Being a wide transformation, it conceptually dumps all eight records into the network and redeals them round-robin into exactly two partitions. The log warns that eight records were shuffled, which is the real cost.

Step 2: The round-robin dealing produces two evenly sized partitions of four records each, regardless of the original skew. This even balance is the benefit of repartition and is exactly what you want before a heavy join so each task has equal work.

Step 3: Coalesce to two is called on the original skewed partitions. Being a narrow transformation, it moves no records across the network; it simply stitches the three existing partitions into two groups in place. The log notes no shuffle, which is the cheapness benefit.

Step 4: Because it only merges existing partitions, the result is uneven — one merged partition ends up with the big six-record partition plus a small one, totalling seven, and the other holds the remaining single record. This unevenness is the trade-off of coalesce, and it only decreased the count.

Step 5: Coalesce to five is attempted. Because coalesce cannot increase the partition count without a shuffle, it has no effect and returns the original three partitions unchanged, demonstrating the decrease-only limitation.

Step 6: The journey makes the contrast concrete — repartition pays a shuffle to produce even, flexible partition counts, while coalesce is free but can only reduce and leaves partitions as uneven as the originals.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Repartition and coalesce both change the number of partitions, but they work in opposite ways and I choose between them based on cost versus balance. Repartition is a wide transformation, so it performs a full shuffle: every record is sent across the network and dealt round-robin into exactly the number of partitions I ask for, which means the output is perfectly even regardless of how skewed the input was, and because it is a real shuffle it can increase the partition count, decrease it, or rebalance while keeping the count the same. The price is the shuffle itself — network transfer, disk writes, and serialization — so repartition is expensive, but I get balanced partitions.

Coalesce, when reducing partitions, is a narrow transformation, so it does no shuffle. Instead of redistributing records, it stitches existing partitions together on the same executors, which makes it very cheap. The trade-offs follow directly from having no shuffle: coalesce can only decrease the partition count, because without moving data it cannot create new partitions, and the output can be uneven, because it just merges whatever partitions existed, so if those were different sizes the merged ones are too. A detail worth stating is that coalescing to a larger number than the current count has no effect unless you pass the shuffle flag, which turns it back into a repartition.

In my project at the National Bank of India I used each for its purpose. After filtering a large daily slice down to a small result spread across two hundred tiny partitions, I used coalesce to reduce it to a handful cheaply before writing the output files, since paying for a shuffle there would be wasteful. Before a heavy join on a skewed dataset, I used repartition to produce balanced partitions so every task had equal work and no straggler dominated, and I also used repartition to raise parallelism on a large dataset. The one caution I always add is that coalescing to very few partitions also shrinks the parallelism of the stage producing the data, so if I coalesce to one before an expensive computation that whole computation runs in a single task — in that case I coalesce after the heavy work or use repartition to keep parallelism while still controlling the output.
